name: Being a Hero on the Weekends
author: Unknown; copies appeared across Shelf-district notice boards in 2197
description: A hand-typeset manifesto, printed on gray recycled stock in runs of approximately forty copies each, that appeared on community boards across Shelf districts 7, 11, and 14 throughout late 2197. No author is claimed. The document is not a call to action and does not offer solutions. It is an attempt to describe, with precision and without self-flattery, the ethical reality of freelancer labor in the informal economy — specifically the way that harm and protection coexist in a single working life. It has been reprinted, quoted, and argued over in equal measure. Some readers find it honest. Others find it an elaborate excuse. The document itself seems to anticipate both reactions.
body:
I protected a family from an eviction crew on a Tuesday. Three kids in that unit, youngest maybe four years old, and when the Arcturus sub-contractors came through the stairwell with their sound gear and their cheap flex-restraints I was the one standing in the corridor and they left. The family got their thirty days. I got Φ340 and a vouch from their building rep.

On Sunday I took a contract to hardwire a killswitch into the inventory management system of a mid-tier distribution warehouse in the Narrows. I didn't know whose warehouse. I didn't ask. I know how to tell myself I didn't know, which is a different thing. When a system like that goes down it usually means delayed shipments, spoiled perishables, and somewhere between eight and thirty people losing contract hours they can't recover. I got Φ1,100 for four hours of work.

I am not telling you this to confess. I am telling you this because I think most of us already know this about ourselves and we have developed an extremely sophisticated set of ways to not look at it directly.

Here is what it feels like from the inside: it does not feel like contradiction. That is the thing nobody tells you. Tuesday and Sunday are separated by five days and three other jobs and the specific texture of needing to eat and cover rack rent and keep my neural overlay subscription current because without it I am effectively deaf to half the communications infrastructure that gets me work. By Sunday the Tuesday family is not gone from my memory, exactly, but it is not present in the way that would make the warehouse job feel like betrayal. The brain is very good at this. I don't think that's weakness. I think that's how a person survives doing two things at once.

But surviving it is not the same as it being okay.

So let me try to think about it straight.

The argument I hear most often goes like this: I only take contracts that don't directly hurt people. No wet work. No targeting civilians. I have lines. And this is true for a lot of us, and the lines are real, and they matter. But the warehouse job didn't cross any of those lines and it still hurt people, just at a distance, just diffused across enough bodies that no individual harm is legible enough to feel like a choice I made. Harm reduction as an ethics only works if you can actually trace the harm. Most of the time you can't. Most of the time the harm is downstream and probabilistic and you are one node in a chain that doesn't show you the whole picture because showing you the whole picture is not in anyone's interest except yours.

The other argument: I don't have a choice. And here I want to be careful because I think this argument is both true and used dishonestly, sometimes in the same sentence.

It is true that refusing dirty contracts is, in significant part, a luxury. If you are C-tier, if you are six weeks into the Signal with one vouch and a borrowed toolkit, you do not get to be principled. You take what clears and you survive or you don't. The freelancers I know who maintain clean contract records are mostly A-tier and above, with enough accumulated reputation that brokers bring them work instead of the other way around. They can say no. The saying no is real. But the ability to say no was purchased with years of saying yes, and what did they say yes to in those years, and should that cost be invisible now that they've cleared it? I know people walking around with genuinely clean hands right now who have clean hands because someone else has dirty ones, because the economy requires dirty contracts to exist and the market is stratified enough that the people with options are not the people who fill those slots.

So: refusing is not neutral. Refusing is a redistribution of who does harm, not an elimination of it.

This is the part where I am supposed to say: and therefore we need systemic change, and therefore individual ethics is a distraction from structural analysis. I have heard this argument. I find it correct and completely useless. Systemic change is not arriving on any timeline that helps the warehouse workers who lost their hours last Sunday. Structural analysis does not make the Tuesday family's thirty days less real. I am not interested in consoling myself with a politics that operates at a scale I will never see.

What I am left with is this: harm reduction that is honest about its limits.

Which looks like: I know the warehouse job hurt people and I took it because I needed to and I did not lie to myself about the first part while doing the second part. I did not tell myself it was probably fine. I did not tell myself the company deserved it or the workers would be okay or someone else would have taken the contract anyway. Someone else would have taken the contract anyway — that's probably true. It does not make it not my harm.

Which also looks like: I did the Tuesday job. I did it well. The youngest kid didn't see anyone get restrained. That was real and it mattered and I am not going to hollow it out by saying it doesn't count because I'm compromised. The people we protect do not become less protected because we are impure. The good we do is not canceled by the harm we do. This is not permission. This is just how addition works.

I think about the people who drop out. Who decide they're done with the informal economy, done with the moral complexity, done. Some of them go corporate — take a staff position, put on a uniform, accept that they will hurt whoever the uniform tells them to hurt but at least the orders are clear and the rack rent is covered. Some of them just go quiet, take low-risk courier and escort work, stay small, stay clean. I respect both choices and I notice that both of them require either institutional protection or a tolerance for poverty that most of us are not going to maintain forever. The moral clarity is real. The cost is real. It is a choice and I will not pretend it isn't, and I will not pretend it's available to everyone who wants it.

I don't have a conclusion.

I have this: I think the most honest thing a freelancer can do is know what they are doing and refuse to not know it. Refuse the story where Tuesday cancels Sunday or Sunday cancels Tuesday. Carry both. It is heavy and it does not resolve and the weight of it is, I think, the closest thing to an ethical life that this particular existence allows.

That might not be enough.

I don't know what enough would look like. I've been trying to figure that out for four years and the answer keeps being another Tuesday and another Sunday and the space between them where I try to be the kind of person who deserves the first one.

Maybe that's all any of us are doing. Maybe that's not a comfort. I wrote this down because I needed to see if it was real when it was outside my head. It looks real. I don't know if that helps.

Leave this where someone else can find it.
